# Package name

package general description

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
```

```{r setup}
library(biodogma)
```

## makeseq()

The "makeseq" function takes a positive integer number as its argument, and creates a randomly generated sequence made of nucleotides.

You can use it as follows:

```{r}
makeseq(sequence_lenght)
```

The output depends on both the size of the sequence to make and the random sampling. Two sequences of the same length could be completely different. Here's an example:

```{r}
sequence_1 <- makeseq(10) 
sequence_2 <- makeseq(10)  

#Outputs: 
print(sequence_1) 
print(sequence_2)
```

## trans()

*`trans()`* substitutes the thymine base (T) of a DNA sequence with a uracil base (U), creating an RNA sequence. It consists of one argument `pattern` where the user inserts the DNA sequence.

```{r}
trans(pattern = "TGCAGTT")
```

## dividing_codons()

dividing_codons function takes RNA sequence (string), counts where the codon should start and divides the sequence into reading codes.

```{r}
dividing_codons("AAUUGGCC")
#>[1] "AAU" "UGG"
```

The function identifies two complete codons, AAU and UGG. The remaining two nucleotides, CC do not form a complete codon and are excluded.

## find_aa()

The `find_aa()` function translates an RNA codon into its corresponding amino acid using the package's codon_table lookup table. It accepts one or more codons as input and returns the associated amino acid abbreviations as a character string.

Examples

```{r}
find_aa(codons = "UUU")
```

The codon UUU encodes phenylalanine, represented by the one-letter abbreviation F.

The function can also accept multiple codons:

```{r}
find_aa(codons = c("UUU", "AUG", "GGU"))
```

Here, UUU encodes phenylalanine (F), AUG encodes methionine (M), and GGU encodes glycine (G). The function concatenates the results into a single character string.

`find_aa()` can be used to translate codons obtained from an RNA sequence-processing function, allowing users to convert codon data into amino acid representations.

## count_plot()

The function takes in the sequence of amino acids as a parameter and counts the appearance of each amino acid.

It is done by defining the unique amino acids from the sequence into a new variable and then counting the number of times they appear in the sequence. The data frame is created storing those counts.

The results are returned in a form of a barplot visualizing the amino acids counts.

Example:

```{r}
count_plot('AKLMAKKK')
```
